title: The morning adhkar
tomorrow: the espresso machine hisses, the rush is on. who stops at noon?

segments.voice: Fajr: the call that talks to someone still in bed. Prayer is better than sleep. Now, the few quiet minutes right after it.

Plenty of phones get checked before feet touch the floor. Amira's Dadi has a different first five minutes. After Fajr she sits on the porch in the dark with her tea and says the same words she says every morning, some of them three times over. Those are the morning adhkar, the remembrances. And in Amira's house they've started a small argument: Amira says hers on the bus, well after sunrise. Dadi says that's too late. Two real views, both inside the tradition.

segments.voice: First, what's being said. Adhkar is the plural of dhikr, remembrance. One, kept in Sahih Muslim, begins: we have entered the morning, and the whole dominion has entered it too, belonging to God. Another, in Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, is said three times: in the name of God, with whose name nothing on earth or in heaven can harm. The Qur'an gives the reason in Pickthall's words: "Remember Allah with much remembrance. And glorify Him early and late." Now the two views. Dadi's: the morning adhkar belong between Fajr and sunrise. The Qur'an pairs glorifying God with the time before the sun rises, and those dark minutes are the seam between night and day, before anything else has claimed you. Say them then, and they open the day instead of interrupting it. Amira's, and some scholars hold it too: morning in Arabic runs past sunrise into the forenoon, and the reports say only "when you reach the morning". So the window is wider, and a person on an early bus or a dawn shift is still inside it. Both agree on more than they argue about. The words are the same. And both would rather you say them late than skip them.

segments.voice: Take a scrap of paper and write one morning line by hand, slowly. If it's yours, the line from Sahih Muslim: we have entered the morning, and the dominion belongs to God. If it isn't, one plain sentence naming what this morning has already given you. Then rest your hand on it while the time runs.

segments.voice: The morning adhkar: remembrances said after Fajr, some of them three times, to open the day with God's name before anything else does.
Something for the bus ride: morning, remembered, before the day starts talking. Two views, the same words.

howItsDone: After Fajr, Muslims who keep the morning adhkar recite set remembrances from the hadith, some once and some three times, often from a small booklet or from memory; scholars differ on whether the window ends at sunrise or runs through the forenoon.

fork.setup: you've always heard the morning adhkar only count before sunrise. state the wider view at its strongest.
options: the time never matters; any hour of the day can be morning.
morning in Arabic runs into the forenoon, and the reports only say when you reach the morning.
the adhkar are optional anyway, so the window doesn't matter.
fork.reveal: the wider view's best case is the language and the reports themselves. the other view's best case is the Qur'an's 'before the rising of the sun'. both say the same words.

original.note: Arabic: the remembrances of the morning; adhkar is the plural of dhikr.

what a scholar hears: the timing debate, Fajr to sunrise or into the forenoon, turns on the Qur'an's 'before the rising of the sun' and the meaning of sabah, morning.

chat.says: dadi says my morning adhkar on the 7:30 bus 'don't count.' who's right??
options: Scholars differ. Dadi's view is before sunrise; others allow the whole morning.
Dadi. After sunrise they're just words, so skip them until tomorrow.
You. Timing doesn't matter at all; any hour of the day is morning.
chat.meaning: Both views are real: before sunrise, or through the forenoon. Same words either way, and late is better than skipped.

adhkar.meaning: remembrances: short set phrases recalling God
